title: Yudhishthira on the riverbank
hook: the war is won, the funeral rites are done, and the new king falls down on the riverbank and can't get up
carry: mourning has its days; then dharma calls you up

segments.voice: Yesterday Bhishma asked Krishna's leave and let go, his eyes on Krishna. Your line was at the last breath, hold God's name.

The water offerings for Bhishma have been poured into the Ganga. The great teacher is gone. Yudhishthira has listened to him at length, about kingship, duty and peace. He has the crown and the kingdom. And at the riverbank, in Ganguli's telling, he simply goes down, collapsing on the bank, overwhelmed by grief. Bhima holds him. Krishna speaks to him. And the old blind king Dhritarashtra, whose own sons died in this war, is the one who tells him to get up. A new book opens with a king on the ground.
screen: `THE OFFERINGS ARE POURED.` → `THE KING FALLS ON THE BANK.` → `THE BLIND KING SAYS: GET UP.`

segments.voice: Ashvamedhika is the book of the ashvamedha, the horse sacrifice: a great royal rite in which a consecrated horse wanders free, guarded by warriors. The idea isn't Yudhishthira's. He wants to leave the throne for the forest. It's the sage Vyasa who tells him grief can't be the whole of a king's life. Perform sacrifices, Vyasa says, give gifts, take up your work; the horse sacrifice will cleanse what weighs on you. Yudhishthira's answer is practical. The war has emptied the treasury, and he will not squeeze grieving people for more. So Vyasa points to old King Marutta, whose sacrifice in the Himalayas was so lavish that the gold left behind is still there. Go and bring it. Here's the Hindu shape underneath. Grief is given real room: the water offerings, the days of rites, the family sitting together. But it has a shape and an end. Many Hindu families keep ten to thirteen days of mourning after a death, closed with a ceremony, and then the household goes back to its work, its pujas, its festivals. The return isn't forgetting. It's dharma calling the living back up, and it often begins, as Vyasa says, with giving: feeding guests and priests, gifts in the name of the one who died. The book of the horse begins on the ground, with a blind king who lost every son telling the winner to stand.
screen: `ASHVAMEDHA: THE HORSE SACRIFICE` · `VYASA: TAKE UP YOUR WORK` · `MARUTTA'S GOLD IN THE MOUNTAINS` · then, large: `MOURNING HAS ITS DAYS, THEN DHARMA CALLS`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone you've lost, or someone near you who is grieving. Breathe in and give the grief its room; nothing needs fixing. Breathe out and ask: what's one ordinary duty I could take up again, gently, in their honor? If you pray, light a small lamp or offer it in their name; if you don't, simply hold them in mind as you do it.
Ashvamedhika. The book of the horse sacrifice, which begins with a grieving king and an empty treasury.
Your line: mourning has its days; then dharma calls you up. The book of the horse begins on the ground. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: The Ashvamedhika Parva is the book of the Mahabharata that follows Bhishma's teachings; Hindus hear it in recitations of the full epic, and the horse sacrifice is remembered as a great royal rite of the Vedic world.

fork.setup: you're Vyasa. Yudhishthira has mourned, and still wants to run to the forest. what do you tell him?

chat.meaning: After Bhishma's rites, Yudhishthira collapses in grief, and Vyasa calls him back to a king's work. Hindu mourning has its days, then the family returns to dharma.
